say: This is a company's admin audit log: who granted access, who rotated a key, who exported data.
Normally it lives in a database an admin can edit. After an incident, the log is the first thing that gets cleaned up, and the auditor has to trust the operator's export.
Witness fixes that without publishing anything readable.
Here is one entry on Arkiv's explorer. Three attributes: a random log id, a counter, and a hash.
The payload is ciphertext. No names, no actions. The key never touched a server, it is in the URL fragment of the share link.
The auditor needs only the writer's address and the log id. The app reads straight from Arkiv, no backend of ours.
It filters by creator, the immutable on-chain creator, so it only trusts entities that wallet wrote.
It recomputes the hash chain from genesis. With the key, the entries decrypt. Without it, they are just bytes.
Anyone can copy our attributes onto their own entity. A look-alike from another wallet is ignored and counted, because its creator is not the writer.
Entries are read-only, so nobody can patch them. The owner could still delete one, and the check shows a gap at that sequence number.
The seal catches a deleted tail too.
Append an event. One atomic batch: the entry and a seal over the new head. The page updates over a websocket, no refresh loop.
Entries live fourteen days, seals ninety, so a deleted tail stays detectable after entries expire.
Entries are created so anyone can extend them. The auditor clicks Renew, and a range query on expiry finds exactly what is about to disappear.
On Postgres the operator rewrites history. On IPFS there is no creator, no expiry, no query. A subgraph is an indexer someone runs.
Here the creator, the read-only flag, the expiry and the query all come from the chain. What stays off Arkiv: the key and the plaintext.
